clue.text: They're dippy

parts.note: dippy reads as daft, but here it means people who take a dip in the sea or a pool

explanation.surface: A dismissive remark about some silly people.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Dippy' suggests foolishness; the cryptic reading is literal, people who go for a dip.
explanation.definitionFit: Swimmers who take a dip are, literally, dippy folk.

clue.text: To impersonate nine dazes one

parts.note: to be someone is to play or impersonate them
the Muses were nine goddesses of the arts in Greek myth

explanation.surface: Acting out nine roles leaves a performer confused.
explanation.definitionFit: To bewilder or confuse someone is to leave them in a daze.

clue.text: Trot aft, it looks like the Revenge

indicators.note: these words, rearranged, look like the answer, signalling a reshuffle of the letters

explanation.surface: Sailing directions aboard a ship named the Revenge.
explanation.walkthrough: 'looks like' rearranges TROTAFTIT. The Revenge was a famous Elizabethan warship, which steers the surface toward ships.
explanation.definitionFit: Retaliation in kind, blow for blow, is a form of getting even.

clue.text: It's legal to bar bad poets

indicators.note: bad suggests the letters are in poor order and must be rearranged

explanation.surface: A claim that it is lawful to ban incompetent poets.
explanation.walkthrough: 'bad' rearranges POETS. 'It's legal' marks the definition as a legal term.
explanation.definitionFit: In law, to preclude a person from asserting something is to bar or prevent them.

clue.text: A pen is not this bird

definitions.text: A pen is not this bird

parts.words: A pen is not this bird
parts.note: a pen is a female swan, so it is not some other bird; but an office worker uses a pen, and there is an African bird named after such a worker

explanation.surface: A naturalist's note that the female swan differs from another bird.
explanation.walkthrough: A pen is a female swan; the secretary bird of Africa has quill-like crest feathers, like pens tucked behind a clerk's ear.
explanation.definitionFit: The long-legged African bird of prey has a crest resembling quill pens behind an office clerk's ear.

clue.text: In that Diogenes was a sponger ?

definitions.text: In that Diogenes was a sponger ?

parts.words: In that Diogenes was a sponger ?
parts.note: the Greek philosopher Diogenes famously lived in a tub, and a sponger here is someone who uses a sponge to wash, not a freeloader

explanation.surface: A remark that the beggar-philosopher Diogenes was a freeloader.
explanation.walkthrough: Diogenes the Cynic lived in a large tub and begged; 'sponger' pretends to mean scrounger but means a person washing with a sponge, and a tub is where one does so.
explanation.definitionFit: A tub for washing is where someone wielding a sponge would sit, and Diogenes made his home in a tub.

clue.text: Blows on the forehead

explanation.surface: Knocks to the head.
explanation.definitionFit: Loud knocks or hits are bumps; a fringe of hair cut straight across the brow has the same name in America.

clue.text: Jovial paper ?

parts.note: jovial means cheerful, but here means of Jove, the god of storms, and a London daily was nicknamed after him

explanation.surface: A cheerful newspaper.
explanation.walkthrough: Jove (Jupiter) hurled thunderbolts; The Times was nicknamed The Thunderer.
explanation.definitionFit: Jupiter's title as god of storms was given as a nickname to The Times newspaper.

clue.text: It was on Rupert Brooke's proposed route to Wendover

definitions.text: It was on Rupert Brooke's proposed route to Wendover

parts.words: It was on Rupert Brooke's proposed route to Wendover
parts.note: in Brooke's poem The Chilterns the speaker plans to walk the road to Wendover, passing a Hertfordshire town on the way

explanation.surface: A question of literary geography about a poet's walk.
explanation.walkthrough: In The Chilterns Rupert Brooke's speaker heads along the old road through the Chiltern Hills to Wendover, passing a market town in Hertfordshire.
explanation.definitionFit: The Hertfordshire market town lies on the road to Wendover named in Brooke's poem.

clue.text: Good weather in Spain, what a stroke of luck!

explanation.surface: Delight at sunny Spanish weather.
explanation.walkthrough: In Spanish the word means fair weather at sea, the origin of the English sense.
explanation.definitionFit: Spanish uses the word for calm, fair weather; in English it is a sudden windfall of good fortune.

clue.text: Word and music

parts.note: mot is French for word
et is French for and

explanation.surface: A heading for a song: lyrics and tune.
explanation.walkthrough: Both pieces are French: mot and et; the music is a short choral composition.
explanation.definitionFit: A motet is a piece of sacred choral music.

clue.text: Roman tank

explanation.surface: A description of an ancient army's armour.
explanation.definitionFit: A centurion commanded a hundred men in the Roman army; the Centurion was a British battle tank of the 1940s-60s.

clue.text: News to end all newspapers

parts.note: sounds like a story that kills off the press, but means the late item squeezed in as the paper is being printed

explanation.surface: A claim of a scoop so big it finishes off the newspaper industry.
explanation.walkthrough: 'To end all newspapers' means at the very end of the paper, the last-minute column added as the presses roll.
explanation.definitionFit: The late-news column in a paper is added after the main pages are set, when the machines are halted.

clue.text: Energy in an Israelite city was idolized

definitions.note: a verb phrase standing for a noun: the definition names the god as the one who was worshipped

indicators.note: in tells us the energy word goes inside the city's name

parts.note: Dan was an ancient city of Israel, at its northern limit
go means energy or vigour

explanation.surface: A biblical-sounding report that vigour in an Israelite town was worshipped.
explanation.walkthrough: The definition is loose: the clue's verb phrase stands for the Philistine god, the one who was worshipped as an idol.
explanation.definitionFit: Dagon was a Philistine deity whose image was worshipped in temples, according to the Bible.

clue.text: Piggeries may be built here

parts.note: reads as a planning note about pig farms; it hints at locations for building, and those letters are those of pigsties rearranged

explanation.surface: A planning note about where pig farms are allowed.
explanation.walkthrough: The answer is the letters of STIES (piggeries) built anew, and is also where any building goes.
explanation.definitionFit: Plots of land on which buildings are put up are building locations.

clue.text: Student shouts, "Appeasement — offer not enough!"

parts.note: a sop is an offering made to appease someone
ho is a shout to attract attention
more is the cry of someone who has not had enough

explanation.surface: A student demonstrator rejects a concession as inadequate.
explanation.walkthrough: The three pieces are all exclamations: a sop offered, 'Ho!', and 'More!'. A sophomore is a second-year student in America.
explanation.definitionFit: In the US a second-year undergraduate or high-school pupil is given this name.

clue.text: Scott's fair maid was not Miss this

definitions.text: Scott's fair maid was not Miss this

parts.words: Scott's fair maid was not Miss this
parts.note: Walter Scott wrote The Fair Maid of Perth, about Perth in Scotland, not the Perth in a southern continent, so she cannot have won that country's beauty title

explanation.surface: A remark about a novel's heroine and a beauty contest.
explanation.walkthrough: Scott's 'Fair Maid of Perth' came from Scotland; there is another Perth in Australia, so she was not 'Miss Australia'.
explanation.definitionFit: The country with its own Perth, in Western Australia, holds its own beauty pageant.

clue.text: With the country upset by attack, there's more to pay

indicators.note: in a down clue upset turns the country's name upside down, so it reads backwards

parts.note: Rus is an old name for Russia
a charge is a rushing attack

explanation.surface: Troubles abroad and an assault lead to higher bills.
explanation.walkthrough: In a down clue 'upset' turns the country's old name upside down; 'more to pay' is an extra charge on a bill.
explanation.definitionFit: An extra fee added on top of the usual price means paying additional money.

clue.text: Tall Jane by the seaside

parts.note: long means tall
Jane Shore was the mistress of the English king Edward IV

explanation.surface: A tall woman named Jane at the beach.
explanation.walkthrough: Jane Shore, mistress of Edward IV, is the historical figure the clue relies on.
explanation.definitionFit: Working or found along the coast is a coastal sense, as in dock workers.

clue.text: One fined for speeding?

parts.note: reads as a motorist with a ticket, but rate can mean speed, and a householder pays the local rates

explanation.surface: A question about a driver caught going too fast.
explanation.walkthrough: Rate means speed, so paying for a rate sounds like a speeding fine; British 'rates' were a local property tax, paid by householders.
explanation.definitionFit: A householder who paid the local property tax, called rates in Britain, was charged for it.

clue.text: Pretty things to snaffle

explanation.surface: A remark about stealing attractive trinkets.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Snaffle' tempts as 'steal', but a snaffle is a horse's bit, and the reins attached to it are called this in coaching slang.
explanation.definitionFit: Decorative strips of satin are pretty adornments; in driving slang the reins fixed to a horse's bit share the name.

clue.text: Some barren ewes can start again

indicators.note: Some says the answer is a run of letters hidden inside the words that follow

parts.note: the letters run across the end of one word into the next

explanation.surface: A farmer's hope that infertile sheep might breed after all.
explanation.definitionFit: To recommence something is to resume or restore it.

clue.text: A Belgian here — in the absence of Humpty Dumpty?

definitions.text: A Belgian here — in the absence of Humpty Dumpty?

parts.words: A Belgian here — in the absence of Humpty Dumpty?
parts.note: Humpty Dumpty sat on a wall; without him there is nothing on it, the word for a barrier followed by a ring for nought and then on

explanation.surface: A Belgian visitor turns up where the nursery-rhyme egg used to sit.
explanation.walkthrough: With Humpty gone the wall has O (nothing) ON it: WALL, O, ON.
explanation.definitionFit: The French-speaking people of southern Belgium are known by this name.

clue.text: Banish the refuse collector ? That's a chancy game

explanation.surface: An order to sack the binman, then a remark about gambling.
explanation.walkthrough: The first reading splits the answer as an order: 'Bin, go!', the rubbish bin told to leave.
explanation.definitionFit: Split in two, the word is an order sending the waste container away; whole, it is a numbers game of luck played in halls.

clue.text: Product of the north only

parts.note: N is the abbreviation for north

indicators.note: a product is what is made from something, so the following word is remade by shuffling its letters

explanation.surface: A claim that something is made solely in northern parts.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Product of' rearranges the letters of 'only'. The whole clue doubles as the definition: the fibre was first made in the 1930s and is a manufactured product.
explanation.definitionFit: The synthetic fibre is a manufactured product of chemical industry.

clue.text: Let Sarah say her piece again

definitions.text: Let Sarah say her piece again

parts.words: Let Sarah say her piece again
parts.note: reads as a plea to hear Sarah's speech once more; the answer is the practice run of a play, where lines are repeated

explanation.surface: A plea to allow a woman to repeat her speech.
explanation.walkthrough: The letters of SARAH and HER, with an L, appear in the answer, but there is no anagram signal; it is a description of a practice session.
explanation.definitionFit: A practice run of a performance has actors go over their lines again.

clue.text: " The singing masons building of gold "(Henry V)

definitions.text: " The singing masons building of gold "(Henry V)

parts.words: " The singing masons building of gold "(Henry V)
parts.note: a fill-in-the-blank quotation from the Archbishop's speech in Henry V comparing a kingdom to a beehive

explanation.surface: A quotation from Shakespeare's Henry V about bees.
explanation.walkthrough: In Henry V Canterbury compares the honeybees to a kingdom, the bees being 'the singing masons building roofs of gold'.
explanation.definitionFit: The tops of houses that masons put up are what the bees are building in the quotation.

clue.text: Accumulate evidence of an early ungulate

parts.note: AM stands for the morning hours, early in the day
an ass is a hoofed mammal, an ungulate

explanation.surface: A request to gather fossil remains of a primitive hoofed beast.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Early ungulate' sounds palaeontological, but it is just AM plus ASS.
explanation.definitionFit: To gather together or collect a large amount is to pile it up.

clue.text: For a picture of a wealthy shaikh?

definitions.text: For a picture of a wealthy shaikh

parts.words: For a picture of a wealthy shaikh
parts.note: a rich Arab ruler's wealth comes from petroleum, so a portrait of him would use the hue of that wealth, an artist's medium

explanation.surface: A question about painting a rich Arab ruler's portrait.
explanation.definitionFit: Paint made with pigment in linseed medium is a classic material for portraits, and petroleum is a sheikh's wealth.

clue.text: From the first-or was it the chicken?

explanation.surface: The old riddle of which came first, chicken or egg.
explanation.walkthrough: The Latin phrase means literally 'from the egg', hence the chicken-and-egg question.
explanation.definitionFit: The Latin phrase means 'from the beginning'; literally 'from the egg', which might have preceded the hen.

clue.text: Trump calls in play

parts.note: suggests bids at cards, but trump is an old word for trumpet, and these are trumpet flourishes in stage directions

explanation.surface: A card player's bids during a game.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Trump' is the archaic form of trumpet; the answer is a flourish called for in Elizabethan stage directions.
explanation.definitionFit: In Shakespeare's stage directions, trumpet fanfares for an entrance are given this name.

clue.text: Great way to float a Victorian company

definitions.text: Great way to float a Victorian company

parts.words: Great way to float a Victorian company
parts.note: sounds like a fine method of launching a business, but the Great ... was both Brunel's huge steamship, a floating company of passengers, and a railway

explanation.surface: Advice on launching a nineteenth-century business.
explanation.walkthrough: The Great Eastern was Brunel's giant Victorian steamship, and also the Great Eastern Railway, a way of a sort.
explanation.definitionFit: Paired with Great, the word names a famous Victorian ship and railway company.
